question: The international rules of the air are contained in:

options.text: Annex 11
Doc 4444, the procedures for air traffic management
Annex 2
Annex 6

explanation: Annex 2 to the Chicago Convention contains the Rules of the Air, first adopted in 1948.

question: The rules of Annex 2 apply to aircraft bearing the nationality and registration marks of a Contracting State:

options.text: Only within their State of Registry
Wherever they are, overriding any national rules of the State being overflown, including its own State's
Only over the high seas
Wherever they are, to the extent they do not conflict with the rules of the State overflown

explanation: Annex 2 applies to such aircraft wherever they are, to the extent it does not conflict with the rules of the State having jurisdiction over the territory overflown.

question: Over the high seas, the rules of the air that apply are:

options.text: Those of Annex 2, without exception
Those of the nearest coastal State
Those of the State of Registry
Those of the State whose FIR covers the area, with any national differences

explanation: The Council resolved that Annex 2 rules apply without exception over the high seas.

question: An aircraft registered in State A flies over State B. Which rules of the air apply?

options.text: Those of State A only
Those of State B, which take priority
Those of whichever State has the more restrictive rule on each point
Annex 2 only, without any national rules

explanation: When flying over a foreign State, that State's rules of the air apply and have priority. Over its own territory, the State of Registry's rules apply.

question: When in flight, an aircraft must be operated in accordance with the general rules and:

options.text: Both the visual and the instrument flight rules
The rules of the operator's operations manual only
The instrument flight rules only, when in controlled airspace
Either the visual flight rules or the instrument flight rules

explanation: In flight, an aircraft complies with the general rules and either VFR (in VMC) or IFR. On the movement area, the general rules apply.

question: Which statement about the choice of flight rules is correct?

options.text: A pilot may choose freely between VFR and IFR in any weather conditions
A pilot may fly VFR in IMC if radar service is available
A pilot may fly IFR in VMC, but must fly IFR in IMC
A pilot must fly VFR whenever VMC exist

explanation: A pilot may elect to fly IFR in VMC (or be required to by ATS), must fly IFR in IMC, and may fly VFR only where VMC exist.

question: VMC are defined in terms of:

options.text: Flight visibility and horizontal and vertical distance from cloud, by airspace class and level
Flight visibility only, measured from the flight deck
RVR and decision height
Ground visibility and cloud ceiling at the nearest aerodrome only, whatever the class of airspace

explanation: VMC criteria use altitude/flight level, flight visibility and horizontal and vertical distance from cloud for each airspace class.

question: In class C airspace at FL120, what are the VMC minima?

options.text: 8 km flight visibility, clear of cloud and in sight of the surface
8 km flight visibility, 1500 m horizontally and 1000 ft vertically from cloud
5 km flight visibility, 1500 m horizontally and 1000 ft vertically from cloud
5 km flight visibility, clear of cloud

explanation: At and above FL100 (10 000 ft), VMC need 8 km flight visibility with 1500 m horizontal and 1000 ft (300 m) vertical distance from cloud.

question: In class D airspace at 6000 ft AMSL, what are the VMC minima?

options.text: 5 km flight visibility, 1500 m horizontally and 1000 ft vertically from cloud
1500 m flight visibility, 1500 m horizontally and 1000 ft vertically from cloud
5 km flight visibility, clear of cloud and in sight of the surface
8 km flight visibility, 1500 m horizontally and 1000 ft vertically from cloud

explanation: Below FL100 the flight visibility requirement falls to 5 km, with the same 1500 m / 1000 ft distance from cloud.

question: In class G airspace at 2000 ft AMSL over flat terrain, VFR flight needs a flight visibility of 5 km and:

options.text: A ceiling of at least 1500 ft
To remain clear of cloud and in sight of the surface
To remain 600 m horizontally and 500 ft vertically from cloud
To remain 1500 m horizontally and 1000 ft vertically from cloud

explanation: At or below 3000 ft AMSL (or 1000 ft above terrain, whichever is higher) in classes F and G, VMC are 5 km visibility, clear of cloud and in sight of the surface; lower visibility may be allowed for slow aircraft.

question: In multi-crew terminology, the pilot flying (PF) is:

options.text: The pilot handling the radio
The pilot who will make the landing, as decided at the briefing
Always the pilot-in-command
The pilot in charge of the controls for the time being

explanation: The PF is the pilot who for the time being is in charge of the controls; the pilot not flying assists under the multi-crew cooperation concept.

question: Before beginning a flight, the pilot-in-command shall:

options.text: Obtain a weather briefing only for IFR flights
Obtain written permission from the operator's chief pilot and a weather briefing for IFR flights only
Become familiar with all available information appropriate to the intended operation
File a flight plan for every flight

explanation: The PIC must become familiar with all available information appropriate to the intended operation.

question: For flights away from the vicinity of an aerodrome and for all IFR flights, pre-flight action must include:

options.text: A radar service for the whole flight
A flight plan and an ATC clearance
Study of current weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements and an alternative course of action
A check that the destination has a control tower and that a radar service is available along the route

explanation: Pre-flight action for such flights includes a careful study of current weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements and an alternative course of action if the flight cannot be completed as planned.

question: Who has final authority as to the disposition of the aircraft while in command?

options.text: The pilot-in-command
Air traffic control
The State of Registry
The operator

explanation: The pilot-in-command has final authority as to the disposition of the aircraft while in command.

question: When may a pilot depart from the rules of the air?

options.text: When flying VFR in uncontrolled airspace
Only when absolutely necessary in the interests of safety
When the operator's procedures say so, provided ATC is informed before the flight
Whenever ATC is not available

explanation: The rules may only be departed from when absolutely necessary in the interests of safety.

question: What does Annex 2 say about alcohol and flight crew?

options.text: It sets a limit of 0.5 per mille
It forbids drinking alcohol within 24 hours of flight and sets a limit of 0.2 per mille
It sets a limit of 0.2 per mille
No one may act while impaired by alcohol, but Annex 2 sets no numerical blood alcohol limit

explanation: Annex 2 prohibits acting as a crew member while impaired by alcohol, narcotics or drugs but gives no numerical limit. European operational rules set 0.2 per mille.

question: In Europe, the blood alcohol limit for crew members exercising their privileges is:

options.text: 0.2 per mille (20 mg per 100 ml)
0.5 per mille
Zero, measured at the start of the duty period only
0.8 per mille

explanation: European operational rules limit blood alcohol to 0.2 per mille (20 mg/100 ml), roughly a quarter of the UK driving limit.

question: What minimum height applies when flying over congested areas, under the general rule?

options.text: 1500 ft above ground level
A height that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m
1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m of the aircraft, in all cases and by day and night

explanation: The general rule gives no figure: aircraft shall not fly over congested areas or open-air gatherings except at a height allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property. Specific figures come from the VFR and IFR rules.

question: The term "level" is used generally to mean:

options.text: The level assigned by ATC for the cruise
Flight level only
Altitude only
Flight level, altitude or height

explanation: "Level" (aircraft level) means variously flight level, altitude or height.

question: At what levels are flights conducted in terms of flight levels?

options.text: Above the transition level only, and only when cleared to do so by ATC in controlled airspace
Above 3000 ft AMSL
At or above the lowest usable flight level, or above the transition altitude
At all levels in controlled airspace

explanation: At or above the lowest usable flight level (or, where applicable, above the transition altitude), flight levels are used. Below it, altitudes are used.

question: Which rule applies regarding proximity to other aircraft?

options.text: Aircraft must stay at least 500 ft apart vertically and 1 NM apart laterally outside controlled airspace
An aircraft shall not be flown so close to another as to create a collision hazard
Formation flights are prohibited at all times
Aircraft must always stay at least 1 NM apart

explanation: An aircraft shall not be operated in such proximity to other aircraft as to create a collision hazard.

question: An aircraft that has the right of way shall:

options.text: Turn right to increase separation
Climb to pass above the other aircraft
Maintain its heading and speed, while remaining responsible for avoiding a collision
Continue as it wishes, the other aircraft being fully and solely responsible for avoiding a collision

explanation: The aircraft with right of way maintains heading and speed; nothing relieves its PIC of responsibility for taking action, including following ACAS advisories, to avoid a collision.

question: An aircraft obliged to give way shall:

options.text: Avoid passing over, under or in front of the other unless well clear, allowing for wake turbulence
Always pass in front of the other aircraft
Always climb above the other aircraft, keeping at least 500 ft vertical separation until well clear of it
Always descend to pass below the other aircraft

explanation: The aircraft giving way avoids passing over, under or in front of the other unless it passes well clear and takes account of wake turbulence.

question: Two aircraft are approaching head-on and there is a danger of collision. What must they do?

options.text: The faster aircraft gives way by turning right
The higher one climbs and the lower one descends
Each alters its heading to the left
Each alters its heading to the right

explanation: When approaching head-on, each aircraft alters heading to the right. Neither has right of way.

question: Two aircraft of the same kind are converging at about the same level. Which gives way?

options.text: The faster aircraft
The one that has the other on its left
The one that has the other on its right
The aircraft at the lower level

explanation: The aircraft that has the other on its right gives way, normally by turning right to pass behind.

question: An aeroplane and a glider are converging at about the same level. Which gives way?

options.text: The glider
The one that has the other on its right
The faster of the two aircraft
The aeroplane

explanation: Power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to airships, gliders and balloons.

question: An airship and a glider are converging at about the same level. Which gives way?

options.text: The airship
The glider
The one with the other on its right
The one at the lower level

explanation: Airships give way to gliders and balloons; gliders give way to balloons.

question: A glider and a free balloon are converging at about the same level. Which gives way?

options.text: The balloon
The glider
Neither; both turn right
The one with the other on its right

explanation: Gliders give way to balloons, which cannot manoeuvre laterally.

question: A power-driven aircraft converges with an aircraft that is seen to be towing a banner. Which gives way?

options.text: The one with the other on its right
The one at the higher level
The power-driven aircraft
The towing aircraft

explanation: Power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to aircraft which are seen to be towing other aircraft or objects.

question: An aircraft is "overtaking" another when it approaches from the rear on a line forming an angle with the other's plane of symmetry of less than:
explanation: Overtaking means approaching from the rear within 70° of the other's plane of symmetry — at night only the white tail light would be visible.

question: An aircraft overtaking another in flight shall:

options.text: Alter heading to the right and keep clear, whether climbing, descending or level
Climb above the aircraft being overtaken
Alter heading to the left and keep clear
Pass on either side, provided at least 500 ft vertical separation is kept from the aircraft being overtaken

explanation: The overtaken aircraft has right of way; the overtaking aircraft keeps out of the way by altering heading to the right until well clear.

question: An aircraft taxiing on the manoeuvring area sees an aircraft on short final. Which has right of way?

options.text: Whichever ATC gives priority to; there is no rule
The aircraft on final approach
The taxiing aircraft
The one on the right

explanation: Aircraft in flight or on the ground give way to aircraft landing or in the final stages of an approach to land.

question: Two aeroplanes are approaching an aerodrome to land. Which has right of way?

options.text: The one that called ATC first, whatever its level, as long as it reported on final
The one at the lower level, provided it does not cut in front of the other
The faster one
The one at the higher level

explanation: The higher aircraft gives way to the lower, but the lower must not take advantage of this to cut in front of another aircraft on final.

question: A glider and a power-driven aeroplane are both approaching to land. Which gives way?

options.text: The power-driven aeroplane
The one that is faster on the approach
The glider
The one at the higher level, whatever its type

explanation: Power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft give way to gliders when landing.

question: A pilot knows that another aircraft is compelled to land. What must the pilot do?

options.text: Land first to clear the runway
Continue to land, as normal priority applies
Climb and hold overhead until ATC gives a clearance
Give way to that aircraft

explanation: An aircraft aware that another is compelled to land shall give way to it.

question: An aircraft taxiing on the manoeuvring area must give way to:

options.text: Aircraft parked on the apron
Other aircraft taxiing towards the apron
Aircraft taking off or about to take off
Vehicles on the taxiway

explanation: An aircraft taxiing on the manoeuvring area shall give way to aircraft taking off or about to take off.

question: A taxiing aircraft reaches a lit stop bar. What must it do?

options.text: Stop and hold; proceed only when the lights are switched off
Stop only at night or in low visibility
Stop, then proceed with caution if no traffic is visible on the runway in either direction
Continue if cleared to line up

explanation: An aircraft taxiing on the manoeuvring area shall stop and hold at all lighted stop bars and may proceed only when the lights are switched off (and when cleared).

question: Two aircraft are taxiing head-on towards each other on the movement area. What must they do?

options.text: The aircraft nearer the runway has right of way and continues
Both alter course to the left
The larger aircraft continues; the smaller stops
Both stop or, where practicable, alter course to the right

explanation: On the surface, when approaching head-on, both stop or, where practicable, alter course to the right to keep well clear.

question: Two aircraft are taxiing on converging courses. Which gives way?

options.text: The one nearer the apron
The one that has the other on its left, by stopping
The one that has the other on its right
The one that has the other on its left

explanation: On the surface the converging rule is the same as in flight: the aircraft with the other on its right gives way.

question: An aircraft taxiing is being overtaken by another. Which has right of way?

options.text: The larger aircraft
The aircraft being overtaken
The overtaking aircraft
The one nearer to the runway in use

explanation: The aircraft being overtaken has right of way; the overtaking aircraft keeps well clear.

question: Vehicles operating regularly on the manoeuvring area of an aerodrome should be:

options.text: Limited to operating only at night
Escorted at all times by a follow-me car
In two-way radio contact with ATC
Painted red and white

explanation: Annex 2 provides that vehicles operating regularly on the manoeuvring area should be in two-way radio contact with ATC.

question: Between sunset and sunrise, an aircraft in flight must display:

options.text: Anti-collision lights only, if fitted, and navigation lights only in IMC
Anti-collision lights and navigation lights
Landing lights and navigation lights
Navigation lights only

explanation: From sunset to sunrise (or as prescribed), aircraft in flight display anti-collision lights to attract attention and navigation lights to show their relative path.

question: Which lights may not be displayed by an aircraft at night?

options.text: Landing lights
Logo lights on the tail and wing inspection lights in all conditions
Cabin lights
Lights likely to be mistaken for its navigation lights

explanation: No other lights shall be displayed if they are likely to be mistaken for the navigation lights.

question: Between sunset and sunrise, an aircraft moving on the movement area must display:

options.text: Navigation lights
Anti-collision lights only
Landing lights only
No lights unless its engines are running

explanation: At night, aircraft moving on the movement area display navigation lights to indicate their relative path to an observer.

question: At night, an aircraft on the movement area must display lights showing the extremities of its structure unless:

options.text: It is parked with its engines shut down, wherever it is parked on the movement area
It is on a taxiway rather than the apron
It is being towed
It is stationary and otherwise adequately illuminated

explanation: Lights marking the extremities are required unless the aircraft is stationary and otherwise adequately illuminated (e.g. on a lit apron).

question: How must an aeroplane on the movement area show that its engines are running?

options.text: By flashing its landing lights
By displaying lights indicating that fact, such as the red anti-collision light
No lights are needed in daylight
By displaying a steady white light on the tail and flashing the landing lights while the engines run

explanation: Aeroplanes on the movement area with engines running display lights to indicate that fact; red anti-collision lights suffice.

question: An aircraft fitted with anti-collision lights is flying in daylight. Must they be on?

options.text: Only in IMC
Only when flying in controlled airspace
Yes, by day as well as by night
No, only at night

explanation: Aircraft in flight fitted with anti-collision lights shall display them by day as well as by night.

question: When may a pilot switch off or dim flashing lights?

options.text: When they adversely affect the performance of duties or dazzle an outside observer
Never, once the engines are running
When flying in VMC
At any time in daylight, and at night when flying in VMC outside controlled airspace

explanation: A pilot may switch off or reduce the intensity of flashing lights if they affect the satisfactory performance of duties or subject an outside observer to harmful dazzle.

question: Simulated instrument flight may only be carried out:

options.text: In IMC with an instructor
In VMC
At night with a safety pilot
Under IFR in controlled airspace

explanation: Simulated IMC can only be carried out in VMC, since the flight must still comply with VFR while the PF's view is restricted.

question: An aircraft may only be flown under simulated instrument flight conditions if:

options.text: The pilot holds an instrument rating
ATC has given a clearance
Fully functioning dual controls are fitted and a qualified safety pilot occupies a control seat
The pilot holds an instrument rating and the aircraft is flying above 3000 ft above ground

explanation: Simulated IMC requires fully functioning dual controls and a qualified pilot in a control seat as safety pilot.

question: In simulated instrument flight, the safety pilot's field of view is not adequate. What is required?

options.text: A competent observer in communication with the safety pilot, in a position that supplements the view
A second safety pilot in the cabin
The flight must be cancelled
ATC radar monitoring of the flight, with traffic information passed to the safety pilot throughout

explanation: If the safety pilot lacks adequate forward and lateral vision, a competent observer in communication with the safety pilot must occupy a position that adequately supplements it.

subtopic: Flight in the vicinity of an aerodrome
question: An aircraft operated in the vicinity of an aerodrome shall:

options.text: Always join overhead the aerodrome
Only fly the published pattern if the aerodrome is controlled, otherwise join as the pilot prefers
Always follow a right-hand circuit
Conform with, or avoid, the pattern of traffic formed by other aircraft

explanation: Whether or not within an ATZ, it must observe aerodrome traffic, conform with or avoid the traffic pattern, make left turns unless instructed and land and take off into wind as appropriate.

subtopic: Flight in the vicinity of an aerodrome
question: Unless otherwise instructed, when approaching to land and after taking off an aircraft shall make all turns:

options.text: To the left
As the pilot considers best
In the direction of the circuit shown in the signal area only
To the right

explanation: All turns are to the left when approaching to land and after taking off, unless otherwise instructed.

subtopic: Flight in the vicinity of an aerodrome
question: An aircraft shall land and take off into wind unless:

options.text: The pilot prefers a longer runway
Safety, the runway configuration or air traffic considerations make another direction preferable
The aerodrome is uncontrolled
The wind is less than 10 kt, when the pilot may choose any runway direction without any further condition

explanation: Landing and take-off are into wind unless safety, the runway configuration or air traffic considerations determine that a different direction is preferable.

question: A flight plan must be submitted before operating any flight, or portion of a flight, that is to be:

options.text: Flown at night
Longer than one hour or more than 50 NM from the departure aerodrome
Flown with passengers
Provided with air traffic control service

explanation: A flight plan is required for any flight or portion to be provided with ATC service, IFR flights in advisory airspace, flights where required for FIS/alerting/SAR or military coordination, and flights across international borders.

question: An IFR flight in advisory airspace must:

options.text: Remain below FL195
Fly only along advisory routes
File a flight plan
Obtain an ATC clearance from the unit providing flight information service

explanation: A flight plan is required for any IFR flight within advisory airspace, though no clearance is issued.

question: A flight plan may be required by the ATS authority for flights in designated areas to facilitate:

options.text: The issue of NOTAM
Coordination with military units or neighbouring ATS units, avoiding interception for identification
Noise monitoring around aerodromes
The collection of navigation charges only, with no link to the alerting service or military coordination

explanation: The authority may require flight plans in designated areas or routes to facilitate flight information, alerting and SAR, or coordination with military units or adjacent States' ATS to avoid interception.

question: A VFR flight will cross an international border. Is a flight plan required?

options.text: No, if the flight is under VFR
Only if the flight lands in the other State
No, if the flight is in uncontrolled airspace
Yes

explanation: A flight plan is required for any flight across international borders, whatever the flight rules or airspace.

question: Where may a flight plan be submitted before departure?

options.text: To an ATS reporting office
Only to the operator
Only to the aerodrome control tower by radio
To the meteorological office

explanation: Before departure it goes to an ATS reporting office; during flight it is transmitted to the appropriate ATS unit or air-ground station, unless repetitive flight plans are used.

question: Unless otherwise prescribed, a flight plan for a controlled flight should be submitted at least how long before departure?

options.text: 3 hours
30 minutes
60 minutes
10 minutes

explanation: A flight plan for a controlled flight is submitted at least 60 minutes before departure (additional rules apply for oceanic control areas).

question: A flight plan filed in flight must reach the ATS unit concerned at least how long before the aircraft reaches the point of entry into a control area?

options.text: 30 minutes
60 minutes
5 minutes
10 minutes

explanation: A flight plan submitted in flight must be received at least 10 minutes before the aircraft is estimated to reach the entry point into a control or advisory area, or the crossing point of an airway or advisory route.

question: Which item is included in a flight plan?

options.text: The number of crew members licensed for the type
Fuel endurance
Aircraft's maximum take-off mass
Name of the operator's chief pilot

explanation: A flight plan contains items such as identification, flight rules, type, wake category, equipment, departure, EOBT, speed, level, route, destination with EET, alternates, fuel endurance, persons on board and emergency equipment.

question: All changes to a flight plan submitted for an IFR flight must be reported to ATS, except:

options.text: Changes in fuel endurance
Changes of cruising level
Inadvertent deviations
Changes of destination

explanation: All changes for IFR or controlled VFR flights are reported as soon as practicable, except inadvertent deviations (dealt with separately). For other VFR flights, significant changes are reported.

question: Before departure, the fuel endurance or the number of persons on board is found to differ from the flight plan. This is:

options.text: A significant change that must be reported
Not significant if the flight is VFR
Only reported if the difference is more than 10%
Reported only after landing

explanation: Incorrect information on fuel endurance or total persons on board at departure constitutes a significant change and must be reported.

question: A repetitive flight plan may be used for flights operated on the same days of consecutive weeks on at least:

options.text: 5 occasions, or every day for at least 5 days
10 occasions, or every day for at least 10 consecutive days
10 occasions within one calendar month only, all at the same time of day
20 occasions over one year

explanation: RPLs are for regularly operated flights with identical basic features, on the same day(s) of consecutive weeks on at least 10 occasions, or every day over at least 10 consecutive days.

question: For a flight for which a flight plan has been submitted, an arrival report shall be made:

options.text: Only if the arrival aerodrome has no control tower
Within 30 minutes of the ETA, to the ATS unit at the departure aerodrome
As soon as possible after landing, to the ATS unit at the arrival aerodrome
Only if the flight was IFR

explanation: Unless local procedures apply, an arrival report is made in person, by radio or data link as soon as possible after landing; the ATS unit then closes the flight plan.

question: Why is it important to make the required arrival report?

options.text: It is needed to pay landing fees
It updates the pilot's logbook
ATC uses it to plan the next departure slot and to invoice the operator for the flight
Failure can trigger unnecessary search and rescue

explanation: Failure to report arrival may cause serious disruption to ATS and great expense in unnecessary SAR operations.

question: Which item is contained in an arrival report?

options.text: Arrival aerodrome and time of arrival
The registration of the next aircraft to depart
Number of passengers
Fuel remaining

explanation: An arrival report contains the aircraft identification, departure aerodrome, destination aerodrome (in case of diversion), arrival aerodrome and time of arrival.

question: A controlled flight is delayed by 30 minutes beyond its estimated off-block time. What should be done with the flight plan?

options.text: Amend it, or cancel it and submit a new one
Nothing; it stays valid for 2 hours
Notify ATC only on first radio contact
It is automatically cancelled after 60 minutes

explanation: For a delay of 30 minutes beyond EOBT for a controlled flight (1 hour for an uncontrolled flight) the flight plan should be amended or cancelled and a new one submitted.

question: Which time reference is used in air navigation and how are time checks given?

options.text: GMT plus the local offset, to the nearest second
UTC, to the nearest minute
UTC, to the nearest 30 seconds
Local time, to the nearest minute

explanation: UTC is used, expressed in hours and minutes of the 24-hour day beginning at midnight; time checks are given to the nearest minute.

question: An ATC clearance normally contains:

options.text: Route, fuel and alternate only
Aircraft type, mass and passenger numbers
Aircraft identification, weather, runway in use and the expected taxi route only
Aircraft identification, clearance limit, route, levels and other instructions

explanation: A clearance contains the aircraft identification, clearance limit, route, levels and any other necessary instructions (time or expiry, departure manoeuvres, communications).

question: ATC clearances are issued solely for:

options.text: Ensuring terrain clearance for the aircraft
Ensuring that the flight follows the most economic route and remains clear of the terrain below
Expediting and separating air traffic, based on known traffic conditions
Protecting the aircraft from bad weather

explanation: Clearances are issued solely to expedite and separate air traffic, based on known traffic conditions (in the air and on the manoeuvring area).

question: When must an ATC clearance be obtained?

options.text: Only for IFR flights departing from an aerodrome with a control tower, before engine start
Before operating a controlled flight, or a portion of a flight as a controlled flight
Before any flight in any airspace
Only before entering class A airspace

explanation: An ATC clearance must be obtained before operating a controlled flight or portion as a controlled flight, normally requested by submitting a flight plan.

question: The PIC finds an ATC clearance unsatisfactory. What may the PIC do?

options.text: Ignore it and file a complaint later
Change to VFR without telling ATC and continue outside the controlled airspace
Fly the flight plan route regardless
Request an amended clearance, which will be issued if practicable

explanation: The PIC may request an amended clearance, which will be issued if practicable.

question: A pilot reads back a clearance incorrectly. What will the controller do?

options.text: Pass the clearance to the next ATC unit to correct once the aircraft is airborne
Cancel the flight plan
Correct the read-back and repeat the clearance until it is right
Accept it, since the pilot is responsible

explanation: The pilot must read back the clearance exactly; if the read-back is wrong, the controller reads the clearance again until it is correct.

question: A clearance contains the words "cleared via Lambourne 2A arrival". This means the aircraft is cleared to follow:

options.text: The published standard arrival route with that designator
A route to be passed later by the approach controller once the aircraft is within radar coverage
The route as filed in the flight plan
Radar vectors to the Lambourne VOR

explanation: "Cleared via (designation) departure/arrival" refers to a SID or STAR published in the AIP. "Cleared flight planned route" means the route as filed.

question: A flight must deviate from its flight plan because of an emergency needing immediate action. What must the pilot do?

options.text: Declare MAYDAY before any deviation
Take the necessary action and inform ATC as soon as possible
Obtain a clearance before deviating
Squawk 7600 and continue on the flight plan until ATC acknowledges the emergency

explanation: Flight plans are adhered to unless an emergency necessitates immediate action, in which case ATC is informed as soon as possible.

question: ATC must be informed if the average TAS at cruising level between reporting points varies, or is expected to vary, from the flight plan TAS by:

options.text: ±10 kt

explanation: ATS is to be informed if the average true airspeed at cruising level varies or is expected to vary by plus or minus 5% of the TAS given in the flight plan.

question: A revised estimate must be passed to ATS when the estimate for the next reporting point, FIR boundary or destination is in error by more than:

options.text: 10 minutes
5 minutes
2 minutes
3 minutes

explanation: The revised time is notified if the estimate is found to be in error by more than 2 minutes from that notified (or other time prescribed by the ATS authority).

question: How should a controlled flight follow a route defined by VORs?

options.text: Along the defined centreline, changing VORs at the change-over point if one is specified
Along a direct track from departure to destination
Anywhere within 10 NM of the centreline
Along the route but changing VORs at the half-way point in all cases, whatever is published

explanation: A controlled flight operates along the centreline of an airway or directly between facilities, changing reference VORs at the specified change-over point.

question: A controlled flight inadvertently deviates from its current flight plan track. What must be done?

options.text: Take action immediately to regain the track as soon as practicable
Request a new clearance before turning back
Squawk 7700 until back on track
Continue on the new track and inform ATC after landing, as the deviation was unintended

explanation: Action shall be taken immediately to regain the track as soon as practicable.

question: A VFR flight in controlled airspace finds it cannot remain in VMC. What should the pilot do first?

options.text: Squawk 7600 and continue
Continue in IMC under VFR
Change to IFR without asking ATC
Request an amended clearance to continue in VMC, or leave the airspace or land

explanation: The pilot requests an amended clearance enabling the flight to continue in VMC to destination, an alternate, or out of the airspace; if not possible, the pilot notifies ATC of the action being taken to leave the airspace or land.

question: A VFR flight inside a control zone cannot maintain VMC. Besides leaving the zone or landing, the pilot may:

options.text: Continue without ATC permission
Descend below 500 ft to stay clear of cloud
Request a special VFR clearance
Squawk 7000 and continue

explanation: In a control zone the pilot may request special VFR; if that is not appropriate, an IFR clearance may be requested.

question: Unless exempted, a controlled flight must report its position:

options.text: Only when crossing FIR boundaries and on first contact with each new ATC unit
As soon as possible after passing each designated reporting point
Every 30 minutes
Only when asked by ATC

explanation: Controlled flights report as soon as possible after passing specified reporting points, unless told to cease (usually when under radar control).

question: Which item is part of a position report?

options.text: Number of persons on board
Outside air temperature and wind at the reporting point
Fuel remaining
Next reporting point and its ETA

explanation: A position report contains identification, position, time, level, next position and ETA, and the ensuing significant point.

question: In a position report, the level may be omitted when:

options.text: The aircraft is cruising
The aircraft is above FL245
Mode C has been verified
The flight is VFR

explanation: The level may be omitted if SSR Mode C has been verified accurate. If ATC has assigned a speed, it is included.

question: ADS-B Out:

options.text: Is a ground radar that interrogates the aircraft
Broadcasts the aircraft's identity, position, altitude and velocity from an on-board transmitter
Transmits only when interrogated by the controller
Is a voice reporting system for oceanic airspace, used where no radar or data link is available

explanation: ADS-B Out periodically broadcasts identification, position, altitude and velocity; ADS-C sends reports under contracts (periodic, event or on demand).

question: When must a controlled flight advise ATC that it is no longer subject to air traffic control?

options.text: As soon as it ceases to be subject to ATC service
Never; ATC knows from radar
Within 30 minutes of leaving controlled airspace, by telephone to the ATC unit concerned
Only when it leaves the FIR

explanation: A controlled flight advises ATC as soon as it ceases to be subject to ATC service, unless it lands at a controlled aerodrome.

question: An aircraft operating as a controlled flight must maintain:

options.text: Contact by data link only
Continuous air-ground voice communication watch on the appropriate frequency
A listening watch on 121.5 MHz only
Two-way communication only when entering and leaving the airspace, with data link in between

explanation: Controlled flights maintain continuous air-ground voice watch; SELCAL satisfies the listening requirement and voice capability must be kept even where CPDLC is used.

question: How does ATC confirm that an aircraft has a radio communication failure?

options.text: By asking the next unit to try contact
By calling it on 243 MHz only
By asking it to make a manoeuvre visible on radar, or to transmit a signal
By sending an interceptor

explanation: ATC asks the aircraft to execute a specific manoeuvre observable on radar or to transmit a signal to acknowledge, and transmits instructions blind.

question: An aircraft's radio fails while it is in the traffic pattern of a controlled aerodrome. What should the pilot do?

options.text: Keep a watch for visual signals from the control tower and comply with them
Squawk 7700 and land immediately
Climb to 3000 ft above the aerodrome and hold overhead until the tower re-establishes contact
Leave the area and land elsewhere

explanation: A watch shall be kept for instructions issued by visual signals from the tower, and such signals complied with.

question: An IFR flight in VMC suffers a radio communication failure. What should it do?

options.text: Continue to the destination following the flight plan and report arrival by telephone after landing
Climb to the highest cruising level and hold
Squawk 7500 and await interception
Continue in VMC, land at the nearest suitable aerodrome and report its arrival

explanation: In VMC (whatever the flight rules), the aircraft continues in VMC, lands at the nearest suitable aerodrome and reports arrival by the quickest means.

question: An aircraft being radar vectored in IMC loses two-way communication. What should it do?

options.text: Rejoin the flight plan route no later than the next significant point
Climb to MSA and hold until contact is regained
Turn back to the departure aerodrome
Continue on the last heading until fuel runs out

explanation: When vectored, the aircraft proceeds in the most direct manner to rejoin the current flight plan route no later than the next significant point, considering minimum flight altitude, squawking 7600.

question: In IMC, in an area where radar is used, an aircraft with radio failure maintains its last assigned speed and level (or minimum altitude if higher) for how long before following its flight plan?

options.text: 20 minutes
7 minutes
3 minutes
30 minutes

explanation: In radar areas the aircraft keeps the last assigned speed and level for 7 minutes (from the later of reaching the level, setting 7600 or failing to report), then adjusts according to the filed flight plan.

question: In IMC, outside radar coverage, an aircraft with radio failure maintains its last assigned speed and level for how long after failing to report at a compulsory point?

options.text: 30 minutes
7 minutes
20 minutes
10 minutes

explanation: In non-radar areas the period is 20 minutes after failing to report over a compulsory reporting point; this gives ATC time to resolve conflicts.

question: After the initial period, a radio-failure aircraft in IMC proceeds along the filed route to the navaid serving the destination. What then?

options.text: Proceeds directly to the alternate
Lands straight in without an approach
Begins descent on arrival over it, whatever the time, and lands as soon as possible
Holds over it, if needed, until it is time to begin descent

explanation: It continues to the appropriate navaid serving the destination and, when required, holds over it until commencement of descent.

question: A radio-failure aircraft has received and acknowledged an EAT. When does it start its descent from the holding navaid?

options.text: When the fuel reaches the reserve amount
10 minutes after arriving over the navaid
At, or as close as possible to, the EAT
At its flight plan ETA

explanation: Descent starts at or close to the last EAT received and acknowledged; if no EAT was acknowledged, at or close to the ETA from the current flight plan.

question: After its approach, a radio-failure aircraft should land, if possible, within what time of the ETA or last acknowledged EAT, whichever is later?

options.text: 30 minutes
10 minutes
60 minutes
20 minutes

explanation: It completes a normal instrument approach and lands, if possible, within 30 minutes after the ETA or last acknowledged EAT, whichever is later, then reports to ATC.

question: An aircraft subject to unlawful interference should try to notify the ATS unit:

options.text: Only after landing
Only by squawking 7700
Only through the operator's company frequency, so that other aircraft are not alarmed
Of the situation and any intended deviation from the flight plan

explanation: It should notify ATS of the fact, significant circumstances and any intended deviation so ATS can give priority and minimise conflict.

question: Unless conditions on board dictate otherwise, an aircraft subject to unlawful interference should:

options.text: Descend immediately to FL100
Keep its assigned track and level until it can notify ATS or is in radar cover
Turn back to the departure aerodrome
Climb to the highest level the aircraft can reach

explanation: The PIC should attempt to continue on the assigned track and level at least until able to notify an ATS unit or within radar coverage.

question: An aircraft subject to unlawful interference must leave its track without being able to contact ATS. What should the PIC do?

options.text: Descend below 10 000 ft to avoid other traffic
Broadcast on 121.5 MHz, squawk 7500 and follow regional contingency procedures
Switch off the transponder to avoid alerting the hijackers and descend below 10 000 ft
Squawk 7600 and maintain the cruising level

explanation: The PIC should broadcast warnings on 121.5 MHz, use on-board systems such as SSR (7500) and data links, and proceed according to regional in-flight contingency procedures.

question: If no regional contingency procedure exists, an aircraft subject to unlawful interference that must leave its track flies at a level that differs from normal IFR cruising levels by:

options.text: 1000 ft where 1000 ft vertical separation is applied, 2000 ft where 2000 ft is applied
300 ft where 1000 ft vertical separation is applied
500 ft where 1000 ft vertical separation is applied, 1000 ft where 2000 ft is applied
500 ft at all levels

explanation: The current text offsets by 150 m (500 ft) where a 300 m (1000 ft) vertical minimum is used and 300 m (1000 ft) where 600 m (2000 ft) is used, putting the aircraft half-way between normal levels.

question: Who may establish procedures for the interception of civil aircraft over a State?

options.text: The military of each State, without reference to any international rules or signals
Only the Organization's Council
Only the State of Registry of the intercepted aircraft
Each State, using the visual signals in the Annex 2 appendix

explanation: Each State has the right to establish interception procedures, but visual signals must be in accordance with Appendix 1 to Annex 2.

question: Concerning interception signals, aircraft on international flights should:

options.text: Carry the interception tables so they can be consulted
Have them memorised by every crew member
Request them from ATC when intercepted
Carry them only when flying over military areas or near prohibited areas

explanation: Aircraft on international flights must carry the interception tables (signals and phraseology) so they can be consulted during an interception.

question: An aircraft is intercepted. What must it do first?

options.text: Continue on its flight plan route
Wait for instructions from ATC before reacting to the intercepting aircraft's signals
Climb away from the interceptor
Follow the intercepting aircraft's instructions, interpreting its visual signals

explanation: The intercepted aircraft immediately follows the instructions of the intercepting aircraft, interpreting and responding to visual signals, and notifies ATS if possible.

question: An intercepted aircraft should try to contact the intercepting aircraft by calling on:

options.text: 121.5 MHz, and if no contact on 243 MHz
406 MHz
The current ATC frequency only, then 123.45 MHz if no contact is made

explanation: It should make a general call on 121.5 MHz giving its identity and the nature of the flight; if no contact, repeat on 243 MHz if practicable.

question: Unless instructed otherwise by ATS, an intercepted aircraft with a transponder should select:

options.text: Mode A 2000 with Mode C
Mode A 7600 with Mode C
Mode A 7700 with Mode C
Mode A 7500 with Mode C

explanation: An intercepted aircraft selects Mode A code 7700 and Mode C, unless otherwise instructed by the ATS unit.

question: An intercepted aircraft receives instructions by radio from another source that conflict with those of the interceptor. What should it do?

options.text: Follow the radio instructions
Request clarification while continuing to comply with the interceptor
Follow whichever instruction the PIC considers safer, without asking for clarification
Ignore both and continue on the flight plan

explanation: The intercepted aircraft requests immediate clarification while continuing to comply with the intercepting aircraft's instructions.

question: An interceptor transmits "DESCEND". What does it mean?

options.text: You are lost, descend
Descend to the minimum safe altitude
Follow me down to the aerodrome below
Descend for landing

explanation: The intercepting aircraft's phrases include CALL SIGN, FOLLOW, DESCEND (descend for landing), YOU LAND and PROCEED.

question: An intercepted aircraft wishes to say "unable to comply". Which phrase does it use?

options.text: WILCO NOT
CAN NOT
UNABLE
NEGATIVE

explanation: The intercepted aircraft's phrases include WILCO, CAN NOT, REPEAT, AM LOST, MAYDAY, HIJACK, LAND and DESCEND.

question: When an ATS unit learns that an aircraft is being intercepted in its area, which action does it take?

options.text: Orders the interceptor to break off
Closes the airspace to all traffic
Tries to contact the intercepted aircraft, e.g. on 121.5 MHz, and informs the pilot
Takes no action, since interception is a military matter

explanation: ATS tries to contact the intercepted aircraft, informs the pilot, liaises with the intercept control unit, relays messages and informs adjacent FIRs if needed.

question: By day, an interceptor rocks its wings from a position slightly above, ahead and normally to the left of the intercepted aircraft, then makes a slow level turn. Meaning?

options.text: You have been intercepted. Follow me
Land at this aerodrome
You are in distress; descend and follow me to the nearest aerodrome
You may proceed

explanation: This is the "you have been intercepted, follow me" signal. At night the interceptor also flashes navigation lights at irregular intervals.

question: How does an aeroplane respond by day to "you have been intercepted, follow me"?

options.text: By climbing and turning away
By flashing its landing lights
By rocking its wings and following
By lowering its landing gear and flashing its landing lights

explanation: The intercepted aeroplane rocks its wings and follows; at night it also flashes navigation lights at irregular intervals. It means "understood, will comply".

question: The intercepted aircraft cannot keep pace with the interceptor. What is the interceptor expected to do?

options.text: Lower its gear and flaps
Fly in front at the slower aircraft's speed with its landing gear lowered
Break off the interception
Fly racetrack patterns and rock its wings each time it passes

explanation: If the intercepted aircraft cannot keep pace, the interceptor flies a series of racetrack patterns and rocks its wings each time it passes.

question: An interceptor makes an abrupt breakaway, a climbing turn of 90° or more without crossing the intercepted aircraft's line of flight. Meaning?

options.text: You may proceed
Land at this aerodrome
Follow me
You are entering a prohibited area

explanation: The abrupt breakaway is the "you may proceed" signal. The intercepted aeroplane responds by rocking its wings.

question: By day, an interceptor circles an aerodrome, lowers its landing gear and overflies the runway in the landing direction. What does it mean?

options.text: The aerodrome is closed
Land at this aerodrome
You may proceed after overflying the runway
Follow me to another aerodrome

explanation: This means "land at this aerodrome"; at night it also shows steady landing lights. The intercepted aeroplane lowers its gear, follows and, if safe, lands.

question: An intercepted aeroplane raises its landing gear while passing over the runway between 1000 ft and 2000 ft above aerodrome level and keeps circling. What does it mean?

options.text: I cannot comply
I will land at this aerodrome after one more circuit
The aerodrome you have designated is inadequate
I am in distress

explanation: This signal (at night, flashing landing lights) means the designated aerodrome is inadequate. The interceptor then either leads it to an alternate or releases it.

question: An intercepted aeroplane switches all available lights on and off regularly, distinct from flashing. Meaning?

options.text: Understood, will comply
Cannot comply
Aerodrome inadequate
In distress

explanation: Regular switching on and off of all lights means "cannot comply"; irregular flashing of all lights means "in distress".

question: An intercepted aircraft flashes all its available lights irregularly. Meaning?

options.text: Cannot comply
Aerodrome inadequate
Understood, will comply
In distress

explanation: Irregular flashing of all available lights means "in distress". The interceptor answers with the series 2 signal ("understood").

question: A VFR flight finds that it can no longer continue in VMC. Which action is acceptable?

options.text: Change the route to stay in VMC
Squawk 7600 and continue
Continue under VFR in IMC
Descend below 500 ft to stay below cloud

explanation: The pilot may land while still in VMC, change route to stay in VMC, file IFR and continue under IFR (if qualified), or, in a CTR, request special VFR.

question: Without ATC authorization, a VFR flight may not take off from an aerodrome in a control zone when the ground visibility is less than:

options.text: 1500 m, or the ceiling is less than 1000 ft
5 km, or the ceiling is less than 1500 ft
5 km, or the ceiling is less than 3000 ft
8 km, or the ceiling is less than 1000 ft

explanation: Unless authorized by ATC, VFR flights shall not take off or land in a CTR, or enter the ATZ or traffic pattern, when the ceiling is below 1500 ft (450 m) or ground visibility below 5 km.

question: VFR flight at night is:

options.text: Allowed only in class G airspace
Allowed without any conditions, provided the pilot holds a night rating
Allowed only as prescribed by the appropriate ATS authority
Always prohibited

explanation: Between sunset and sunrise (or other prescribed period), VFR flights are to be operated in accordance with conditions prescribed by the ATS authority.

question: Unless authorized by the ATS authority, VFR flights shall not be operated:

options.text: Above FL100
Above FL245, or faster than 250 kt IAS below FL100
Above 3000 ft AMSL
Above FL200, or at transonic or supersonic speeds

explanation: VFR flights need authorization to operate above FL200 or at transonic and supersonic speeds.

question: In airspace where RVSM is applied, VFR flights are:

options.text: Not authorized between FL290 and FL410
Authorized only by day
Authorized at VFR levels up to FL410, provided the aircraft has RVSM approval
Authorized only with a transponder

explanation: Authorization for VFR flight is not given in RVSM airspace (FL290 to FL410), freeing those levels for IFR traffic.

question: Except for take-off and landing, a VFR flight over a congested area or open-air assembly of persons shall not be flown below:

options.text: 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m of the aircraft
500 ft above the highest obstacle within 150 m
1500 ft above ground level
1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km of the aircraft's estimated position

explanation: Over congested areas the VFR minimum is 300 m (1000 ft) above the highest obstacle within a radius of 600 m from the aircraft.

question: Away from congested areas, the minimum height for VFR flight is:

options.text: 300 ft above the ground
1000 ft above the ground
500 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m
500 ft (150 m) above the ground or water

explanation: Elsewhere VFR flights shall not be flown below 150 m (500 ft) above the ground or water, except for take-off and landing or with permission.

question: In level cruising flight above the transition altitude, a VFR flight shall be flown:

options.text: At the altitude given in its flight plan, with the regional QNH set
At an IFR flight level appropriate to its track
At a VFR flight level appropriate to its magnetic track
At any flight level the pilot chooses

explanation: Above the transition altitude, VFR flights cruise at VFR flight levels from the table, according to magnetic track (unless ATC assigns otherwise in controlled airspace).

question: In which airspace class is VFR flight not permitted?

options.text: Class D
Class A
Class E
Class B

explanation: VFR flight is not permitted in class A. VFR flights comply with ATC instructions in classes B, C and D, as aerodrome traffic at controlled aerodromes, and when flying special VFR.

question: In item 8 of the flight plan, a flight that starts under VFR and changes to IFR en route is shown by the letter:

options.text: Z
V
I
Y

explanation: V is VFR throughout, I is IFR throughout, Y is IFR first then VFR, and Z is VFR first then IFR.

question: The PIC of a VFR flight that has filed a VFR flight plan wishes to change to IFR in controlled airspace. What must be done?

options.text: Simply start flying IFR and tell ATC later
Pass the flight plan changes and get an IFR clearance before flying IFR
File a new flight plan after landing
Squawk 2000 and continue

explanation: The PIC communicates the changes to the current flight plan (or submits an IFR flight plan) and obtains a clearance before proceeding under IFR in controlled airspace.

question: A VFR flight plan is being filled in. How is the total estimated elapsed time measured?

options.text: From engine start until landing at the destination
From take-off until the initial approach fix at the destination
From take-off until overhead the destination aerodrome
From take-off until entry into the destination's control zone

explanation: For VFR the EET runs from take-off to over the destination aerodrome; for IFR, to the designated point where the instrument approach begins.

question: In which airspace classes may VFR flights operate without two-way radio communication?

options.text: F and G only
D, E, F and G
C, D and E
E, F and G

explanation: Controlled VFR flights must maintain two-way communication; in classes E, F and G, VFR flights may operate without two-way radio.

question: To act as PIC or co-pilot of an aeroplane under IFR, a licence holder must:

options.text: Hold a valid instrument rating appropriate to the aircraft category
Hold an airline transport pilot licence
Have at least 500 hours of total time
Be accompanied by an instructor or a second pilot holding an instrument rating

explanation: A licence holder may not act as PIC or co-pilot under IFR without a valid IR appropriate to the aircraft category.

question: Where no minimum flight altitude has been set by the State, an IFR flight over high terrain or mountainous areas shall be flown at least:

options.text: 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km
2000 ft above the highest obstacle within 5 km
1500 ft above the highest obstacle within 15 km of its estimated position
2000 ft (600 m) above the highest obstacle within 8 km of its estimated position

explanation: Over high terrain or mountains: at least 600 m (2000 ft) above the highest obstacle within 8 km (5 NM) of the estimated position.

question: Where no minimum flight altitude has been set, outside high terrain an IFR flight shall be flown at least:

options.text: 1500 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m of its estimated position
1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 5 km
1000 ft (300 m) above the highest obstacle within 8 km of its estimated position
500 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km

explanation: Elsewhere the minimum is 300 m (1000 ft) above the highest obstacle within 8 km of the estimated position.

question: A flight plan shows the letter Y in item 8. This means the flight will be:

options.text: A special VFR flight
IFR first, then VFR
VFR first, then IFR
IFR throughout

explanation: Y means IFR followed by VFR (I → V); Z means VFR followed by IFR.

question: An IFR flight in VMC wishes to cancel IFR. When should it do so?

options.text: Only if uninterrupted VMC is expected for a reasonable period
Only above FL100
Whenever it is in VMC
Only when ATC suggests it, whatever the weather expected ahead

explanation: An IFR flight shall not cancel IFR unless it is expected that it will continue for a reasonable period in uninterrupted VMC. A change of flight rules is only at the pilot's request ("cancelling my IFR flight").

question: For an IFR flight, the total estimated elapsed time in the flight plan is the time from take-off until:

options.text: The aircraft starts its descent
Landing at the destination
Over the designated point from which the instrument approach will start
Overhead the destination aerodrome, or landing if no navaid serves it

explanation: For IFR the EET runs from take-off to over the designated point (usually the IAF) from which the instrument approach procedure will begin.

question: In controlled airspace, an IFR flight authorised to use cruise climb shall cruise:

options.text: At any level chosen by the pilot
Only at the level in the flight plan
At VFR levels, so as to avoid other IFR traffic at the normal cruising levels
Between two levels, or above a level, selected from the cruising level table

explanation: IFR flights in controlled airspace cruise at a level or, with cruise climb, between two levels or above a level, from the table of cruising levels.

question: An IFR flight outside controlled airspace shall cruise at:

options.text: Any level it chooses
A level appropriate to its magnetic track
The level assigned by the flight information service
A VFR level to show it is uncontrolled

explanation: Outside controlled airspace, IFR flights fly at cruising levels appropriate to their magnetic track (semi-circular rule).

question: An IFR flight outside controlled airspace, in an area where flight plans are required, must:

options.text: Remain below FL100
Fly only along advisory routes
Keep a listening watch with the unit providing FIS and make position reports
Obtain an ATC clearance from the unit providing flight information service

explanation: Such flights establish communication and keep a continuous listening watch with the FIS unit, and make position reports.

question: Under the semi-circular rule, which magnetic tracks count as "eastbound"?

options.text: 000° to 180° inclusive

explanation: Eastbound tracks are 000° to 179° magnetic; westbound tracks are 180° to 359°.

question: How do IFR and VFR cruising levels differ?

options.text: IFR levels are whole thousands of feet; VFR levels are thousands plus 500 ft
They are the same; only the direction differs
IFR levels are thousands plus 500 ft; VFR levels are whole thousands of feet
VFR levels are even thousands only

explanation: IFR levels are whole thousands (e.g. FL70); VFR levels are thousands plus 500 ft (e.g. FL75).

question: An IFR flight is on a magnetic track of 095° below FL290. Which flight level is correct?

options.text: FL75
FL70
FL80
FL60

explanation: Eastbound (000°–179°) IFR levels below FL290 are odd thousands: FL30, 50, 70, 90 and so on. FL75 is a VFR level.

question: A VFR flight is on a magnetic track of 270° above the transition altitude. Which level is correct?

options.text: FL65
FL70
FL55
FL60

explanation: Westbound (180°–359°) VFR levels are even thousands plus 500: FL45, 65, 85 and so on.

question: In RVSM airspace, which flight level is correct for an IFR flight on a magnetic track of 200°?

options.text: FL330
FL320
FL310
FL350

explanation: In RVSM airspace (FL290–FL410, 1000 ft separation), westbound IFR levels are FL300, 320, 340, 360, 380 and 400; eastbound are FL290, 310, 330, 350, 370, 390 and 410.

question: In airspace where RVSM is applied, which is the first westbound IFR level above FL410?

options.text: FL440
FL450
FL430
FL420

explanation: Above FL410, 2000 ft separation returns: eastbound FL450, 490, 530; westbound FL430, 470, 510.

question: Where RVSM is not applied, which is a correct eastbound IFR level above FL290?

options.text: FL320
FL350
FL310
FL330

explanation: Without RVSM, IFR levels above FL290 are 4000 ft apart in each direction: eastbound FL290, 330, 370, 410; westbound FL310, 350, 390.

question: Which equipment and approval does an aircraft need to use RVSM airspace?

options.text: No special equipment
RVSM approval and ACAS
A second transponder only
GNSS and a data link

explanation: Aircraft using RVSM must be approved by the airspace authority and fitted with ACAS (TCAS). Above FL410 altimetry errors are considered too great for 1000 ft separation.

question: What is the highest VFR cruising level in the table, and for which direction?

options.text: FL295, eastbound
FL195, either direction
FL275, westbound
FL285, westbound

explanation: VFR levels run up to FL285 westbound and FL275 eastbound; VFR is not authorized in RVSM airspace above.

question: In which airspace, and in what weather, may a special VFR clearance be given?

options.text: In any controlled airspace at night, in conditions below VMC
In class G airspace, in IMC
Within a control zone, in conditions below VMC
Above FL200, in VMC only

explanation: SVFR is a VFR flight cleared by ATC to operate within a control zone in meteorological conditions below VMC.

question: Special VFR is applicable to flights:

options.text: Into, out of, or within a control zone
In any controlled airspace below 3000 ft
Anywhere in a terminal control area
Along airways below FL100

explanation: SVFR only applies to flights into, out of or within a control zone.

question: Special VFR flight may be authorized within a control zone when the ground visibility is not less than:

options.text: 3 km
5 km

explanation: SVFR may be authorized when the ground visibility within the control zone is not less than 1500 m.

question: A distress message is preceded by:

options.text: MAYDAY, spoken three times
PAN PAN, spoken three times
MAYDAY, spoken twice
SECURITE, spoken three times

explanation: Distress (grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance) is MAYDAY three times. Urgency is PAN PAN three times.

question: Which visual signal indicates distress?

options.text: A white pyrotechnic light
A succession of red pyrotechnic lights
A succession of green pyrotechnic lights
Repeated switching on and off of landing lights

explanation: Distress signals include a succession of red pyrotechnics or a red parachute flare.

question: An urgency message is preceded by:

options.text: URGENT, spoken three times
MAYDAY, spoken three times and followed by the word URGENT
PAN PAN, spoken three times
PAN, spoken once

explanation: Urgency — a message about the safety of an aircraft, ship, vehicle or person on board or in sight — is preceded by PAN PAN three times.

question: A pilot must land because of a problem but needs no other assistance. Which visual signal indicates this?

options.text: A red parachute flare
Rocking the wings
A succession of red pyrotechnics fired at short intervals
Repeated switching on and off of the landing lights

explanation: Repeatedly switching the landing lights (or other lights) on and off shows that the aircraft is compelled to land but needs no immediate assistance.

question: Which transponder code indicates an emergency?
explanation: 7700 is the emergency code, used unless the aircraft has already been identified on an assigned code.

question: Which transponder code indicates radio communication failure?
explanation: 7600 indicates radio failure and should be used whenever it happens.

question: Code 7500 indicates:

options.text: VFR conspicuity
Radio failure
Unlawful interference
Emergency

explanation: 7500 indicates unlawful interference; ATC treats it discreetly unless the pilot mentions it on the radio.

question: Code 7000 is used to indicate:

options.text: An aircraft in a radar area that is not receiving a radar service
A transponder failure
An aircraft in distress
An aircraft entering a radar area from oceanic airspace and requesting a service

explanation: 7000 is the conspicuity code for an aircraft not receiving a radar service, implying VFR flight.

question: Code 2000 is used:

options.text: To indicate VFR flight outside controlled airspace, in an area where radar service is available
When no code has been assigned, e.g. entering a radar area from airspace where none was given
To indicate an unserviceable transponder
To indicate a military flight

explanation: 2000 is used when no ATC instruction or regional agreement has assigned a code, typically on entering radar-controlled airspace from oceanic airspace.

question: Code 0000 indicates:

options.text: A request for radar service
The aircraft has been hijacked but the crew cannot say so on the radio
The aircraft is on the ground
The transponder is unserviceable or inaccurate

explanation: 0000 is reserved to indicate that the transponder is in some way unserviceable or inaccurate.

question: When squawking a reserved code, the transponder should also transmit:

options.text: Mode A only
Mode S only
Mode C (pressure altitude)
Nothing else

explanation: The altitude reporting function (Mode C) should be transmitted together with the code at all times.

question: In what form are prohibited, restricted and danger areas published?

options.text: On ATC radar maps only
Only by NOTAM, each time an area becomes active, with no permanent publication
Only in AICs
In the AIP, designated with P, R or D and a number

explanation: States may establish P, R and D areas for safety or security; they are detailed in the AIP with a code showing type, number and upper limit, and may be permanent or activated by NOTAM.

question: After a danger area is withdrawn, its designator may not be reused for at least:

options.text: 5 years
12 months
6 months
3 months

explanation: An area designator is not re-used for at least 12 months after the area is cancelled, avoiding confusion while charts are reprinted.

question: By day or night, a series of projectiles fired from the ground at 10-second intervals, each bursting with red and green lights, means:

options.text: You are flying in, or about to enter, a restricted, prohibited or danger area
Land immediately at the nearest aerodrome
You are being intercepted and must follow the interceptor to the nearest aerodrome
The aerodrome is closed

explanation: These signals warn an aircraft that it is flying in or about to enter a restricted, prohibited or danger area and must take remedial action.

question: A pilot sees a light signal from the control tower directed at the aircraft. What should the pilot assume?

options.text: That it is only for non-radio aircraft
That it is a test of the lamp
That it is meant for this aircraft, even if it has a radio
That it can be ignored if ATC has already given a clearance by radio

explanation: The signal lamp is narrow-beam and directional, so a signal seen must be assumed to be meant for you. Aircraft with radios must also comply with visual instructions.

question: A steady green light from the tower to an aircraft in flight means:

options.text: Cleared for take-off
Cleared to taxi
Return for landing
Cleared to land

explanation: Steady green: in flight, cleared to land; on the ground, cleared for take-off.

question: A steady green light from the tower to an aircraft on the ground means:

options.text: Return to the starting point
Cleared for take-off
Stop
Cleared to taxi

explanation: On the ground a steady green means cleared for take-off. Flashing green means cleared to taxi.

question: A steady red light to an aircraft in flight means:

options.text: Aerodrome unsafe, do not land
Do not land for the time being
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
Return to the starting point

explanation: Steady red in flight: give way to other aircraft and continue circling. On the ground: stop.

question: A steady red light to an aircraft on the ground means:

options.text: Stop
Return to the starting point
Hold short of the runway
Taxi clear of the landing area

explanation: Steady red on the ground means stop.

question: A series of green flashes to an aircraft in flight means:

options.text: Cleared to taxi
Land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron
Return for landing
Cleared to land

explanation: Green flashes: in flight, return for landing (a steady green will follow as landing clearance); on the ground, cleared to taxi.

question: A series of green flashes to an aircraft on the ground means:

options.text: Cleared to taxi
Taxi clear of the landing area
Cleared for take-off
Return to the starting point

explanation: On the ground, green flashes mean cleared to taxi.

question: A series of red flashes to an aircraft in flight means:

options.text: Give way and continue circling
Aerodrome unsafe, do not land
Do not land for the time being
Return for landing

explanation: Red flashes: in flight, aerodrome unsafe, do not land; on the ground, taxi clear of the landing area in use.

question: A series of red flashes to an aircraft on the ground means:

options.text: Stop
Return to the starting point
Cleared to taxi
Taxi clear of the landing area in use

explanation: On the ground, red flashes mean taxi clear of the landing area in use.

question: A series of white flashes to an aircraft in flight means:

options.text: Land here when cleared (steady green), then proceed to the apron
Cleared to land immediately
Aerodrome closed, divert
Return to the starting point

explanation: White flashes in flight: land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron (landing and taxi clearance to follow as steady green and green flashes).

question: A series of white flashes to an aircraft on the ground means:

options.text: Cleared to taxi to the apron
Taxi clear of the landing area
Stop immediately
Return to the starting point on the aerodrome

explanation: On the ground, white flashes mean return to the starting point on the aerodrome.

question: A red pyrotechnic fired from the tower to an aircraft in flight means:

options.text: You are entering a danger area; leave it by the shortest route
Notwithstanding any previous instructions, do not land for the time being
Aerodrome unsafe, do not land
Give way and continue circling

explanation: A red pyrotechnic means: notwithstanding any previous instructions, do not land for the time being.

question: By day, how does an aircraft in flight acknowledge a light signal from the tower?

options.text: By flashing its landing lights twice
By moving its ailerons or rudder
By rocking its wings
By switching its navigation lights on and off twice

explanation: In flight by day, rock the wings; at night, flash the landing lights (or navigation lights) on and off twice.

question: By day, how does an aircraft on the ground acknowledge a light signal from the tower?

options.text: By flashing its landing lights twice
By flashing its taxi light once
By rocking its wings
By moving its ailerons or rudder

explanation: On the ground by day, move the ailerons or rudder; at night, flash the landing lights (or navigation lights) twice.

question: The absence of a signal area at an aerodrome indicates that:

options.text: The aerodrome is not to be used by non-radio aircraft
The aerodrome is closed
Non-radio aircraft must join overhead
The aerodrome has no control tower and non-radio aircraft must join overhead

explanation: The signal area, visible from the air, passes information to non-radio aircraft; its absence means the aerodrome is not to be used by non-radio traffic.

question: A white landing T is displayed in the signal area. In which direction are take-offs and landings made?

options.text: Parallel to the cross-arm
Parallel to the shaft of the T, towards the cross-arm
Towards the foot of the shaft
In any direction, the T only marks the position of the signal area

explanation: Take-offs and landings are made in a direction parallel with the shaft of the T, towards the cross-arm.

question: A white disc is displayed next to the landing T. It means:

options.text: The aerodrome is closed
Only helicopters may land, on the area marked by the disc
The landing and take-off directions do not necessarily coincide
Gliding is in progress

explanation: A white disc alongside the T indicates that the directions of landing and take-off do not necessarily coincide.

question: A white dumb-bell is displayed in the signal area. It means:

options.text: Aircraft movement on the ground is confined to paved or hard surfaces
Take-offs and landings on runways only, ground movement not restricted
Landing is prohibited
Gliding is in progress

explanation: A plain white dumb-bell confines ground movement to hard surfaces. With black stripes across each disc it means take-off and landing on runways, but ground movement is not confined to hard surfaces.

question: A white dumb-bell with a black perpendicular stripe across each circular portion means:

options.text: Right-hand circuit in force
Landing prohibited
All movement confined to hard surfaces
Runways only for take-off and landing; other movement not confined to hard surfaces

explanation: The striped dumb-bell means take-off and landing on runways only, while ground movement is not confined to hard surfaces.

question: A right-hand arrow in a conspicuous colour displayed in the signal area means:

options.text: Taxi to the right
The runway in use is to the right of the signal area as seen from the air
Turns before landing and after take-off are to be made to the right
Wind is from the right

explanation: The right-hand arrow (e.g. red and yellow striped) means a right-hand traffic circuit is in force.

question: A red square panel with one yellow diagonal is displayed. It means:

options.text: Gliding is in progress
The state of the manoeuvring area is poor; take special care when landing
Landing is prohibited
The aerodrome is closed for the night and landings are prohibited until morning

explanation: One yellow diagonal on a red square means special precautions are needed because of the poor state of the manoeuvring area or another reason.

question: A red square panel with two yellow diagonals (a cross) is displayed. It means:

options.text: Landings are prohibited, and the prohibition is liable to be prolonged
Gliding is in progress
Take special care when landing
Helicopters only may land, on the area marked in the signal area

explanation: A red square with yellow diagonals (a yellow cross) means landing is prohibited and the prohibition may be prolonged.

question: A white H displayed in the signal area means:

options.text: Heavy aircraft are operating
Holding point for helicopters only
A hospital is near the aerodrome and must not be overflown below 1000 ft
Helicopters shall take off and land only within the designated area

explanation: A white H indicates that helicopters shall take off and land only within the designated area.

question: A white double cross in the signal area means:

options.text: Area unfit for movement
Glider flying is in progress
Helicopter operations in progress
Landing prohibited

explanation: A white double cross displayed horizontally in the signal area indicates that gliding is in progress.

question: Crosses of a single contrasting colour displayed on a runway or taxiway indicate:

options.text: The holding position
The touchdown zone
That section is unfit for the movement of aircraft
The end of the stopway or the start of a displaced threshold

explanation: Crosses on a runway or taxiway mark an area unfit for aircraft movement; orange and white markers delimit unusable areas.

question: Which runway-holding position marking is used for the holding point nearest the runway?

options.text: A white transverse stripe
Pattern A: two solid and two dashed yellow lines
A single broken yellow line
Pattern B: a yellow ladder marking across the whole taxiway

explanation: Pattern A (two solid and two dashed lines, dashed on the runway side) marks the holding position nearest the runway. Pattern B (ladder) marks others.

question: Pattern B runway-holding position marking (a ladder) is used:

options.text: For holding positions other than the one closest to the runway
For intermediate holding positions where two taxiways cross each other
For the holding position closest to a visual runway
To mark a road-holding position on a runway

explanation: Pattern B marks holding positions further from the runway, such as CAT II/III holding points behind a pattern A.

question: A black letter C on a yellow background, displayed vertically, indicates:
